title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma

direction.comments: The direction on a macroscale is very much a surrealist film that pays homage to the 1970s and 1980s slasher genre, doing a pretty good job showing how campy this camp is while creating a surrealist world with clear slasher elements; the direction on a microscale is fine as it acts primarily as a two-person movie where the two leads have good chemistry, and it integrates humor effectively throughout the movie; the storytelling allows the movie to be somewhat autobiographical about the director's feelings towards the sexualization of women in movies, their career after I Saw the TV Glow, and the current state of Hollywood (especially resurrecting IP), though the storyline is dragged out to cover all its bases; the tension is built in a campy slasher way, but it is ultimately predictable because this is not a true horror movie but rather a commentary on film, sexuality, and transgender identity

performance.comments: Carries the lead role really well, showing strong emotion, demonstrating great comedic timing from her stand-up background, and sharing excellent chemistry with Gillian Anderson to display the semi-autobiographical feelings of the director

Delivers an enjoyable performance, playing an elder figure dynamic to Einbinder very well; though her Southern accent is a little over the top, her character unlocks something dormant in the protagonist for a key epiphany

cast.comments: Functions effectively as a two-person movie bolstered by a supporting cast that plays their roles well to buttress and support the main duo

story.comments: The concept is interesting, functioning as a slasher film on the surface while using the making of a reboot to explore themes of sexuality, gender identity, and the director's feelings about Hollywood and their career after the success of I Saw the TV Glow, though it can be a little too meta at times; the plot structure is mostly a linear story that interweaves elements of the original 'Camp Miasma' film to help show symbolism, but it has issues with dragging and stretching out the plot through unnecessarily long scenes; character writing is pretty good and somewhat autobiographical, inserting the director's own views of Hollywood, cinema, their previous film, and their own gender and sexuality into the protagonist

screenplay.comments: The dialogue is pretty strong, though a little too meta, appearing a little too on the nose at times but remaining enjoyable to an extent; the humor is pretty good, functioning as a black comedy and a critique of the current climate, landing more laughs than expected; the symbolism is very on the nose as an allegory for gender, sexuality (especially female sexuality in cinema), and commentary that pokes fun at the expectation to follow up the success of I Saw the TV Glow, while still being a trans allegory in itself; the foreshadowing is present throughout the movie, making parts of the film feel a little predictable

score.comments: Lighter in the movie, doing well to complement the surrealist feel and present a couple of themes without being overbearing

soundtrack.comments: Included in the movie but does not play that big of a role overall

cinematography.comments: Well executed, successfully helping create a surrealist feel for the movie and paying homage to 1970s style slasher movies

editing.comments: Complements the 1970s slasher aesthetic and surrealist tone (especially with fades and period techniques), but holds the movie back with unnecessarily long shots and sequences (like the slasher sequence and sex scene in the middle) that drag the film out

sound.comments: Delivers a campy slasher sound scheme congruent with what you would expect from that time period

visual_effects.comments: Intentionally low budget and over-the-top at times to emulate 1970s campy slashers, though the sudden shift to modern CGI slasher effects in the middle sequence feels a bit out of place, despite how campy it is

production_design.comments: Creates a surrealist, low-budget feel emulating 1970s slashers, cleverly acting as a symbolic space for the director to explore identity and sexuality

makeup.comments: Emulates the feel of a low-budget 1970s slasher movie

costumes.comments: Fit the characters and place them appropriately in their respective time periods

review.pacing: Hurts the movie a good amount as it drags heavily (especially in the final 30-40 minutes) due to unnecessarily long shots and repetitive sequences where trimming 10-15 minutes could have made it much tighter and eliminated fluff, because it felt like they were very much trying to fill time
review.climax: Deeply symbolic of the character coming into her own sexuality, but does drag heavily with how repetitive and unnecessarily long it is
review.tone: A fun and entertaining blend of 1970s slasher homage mixed with black comedy and strong social commentary, though it becomes annoying by beating the dead horse of how incredibly meta it is
review.overall: Overall, 'Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma' is a decent commentary piece that uses a surrealist filmmaking style and a 1970s slasher homage as a semi-autobiographical exploration of sexuality, gender identity, and the director's own feelings on following up 'I Saw the TV Glow'; while the dynamic between Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson is strong and the black comedy moments are enjoyable, the film is ultimately held back by being too meta and suffering from poor pacing, with the overt messaging and repetitive, unnecessarily long sequences making the movie feel like it is beating a dead horse
